clinicalPearls: Defects of the interferon-gamma/IL-12 axis cause Mendelian susceptibility to mycobacterial disease (MSMD), a selective vulnerability to weakly virulent mycobacteria

Affected individuals develop disseminated infection with environmental (non-tuberculous) mycobacteria and with the BCG vaccine strain, as well as an increased risk of severe tuberculosis and salmonellosis

The underlying problem is failure of the cytokine circuit by which macrophages and T/NK cells communicate to control intracellular pathogens, involving genes such as IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, and STAT1

IL-12 produced by macrophages normally drives lymphocytes to secrete interferon-gamma, which in turn activates macrophages to kill intracellular organisms; breaking this loop cripples defence against mycobacteria

The clinical severity depends on the specific defect, ranging from complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency with severe early disseminated disease to partial defects with milder, more localised infection
Because the immune defect is narrow, patients are typically not broadly susceptible to the wide range of pathogens seen in combined immunodeficiencies

Complete receptor defects respond poorly to interferon-gamma therapy, whereas partial or IL-12-axis defects may benefit from adjunctive interferon-gamma alongside prolonged antimycobacterial treatment
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is considered for severe complete defects, though outcomes can be challenging
reference.pathophysiology: This group of disorders disrupts the interferon-gamma-dependent axis that controls intracellular pathogens. Following ingestion of mycobacteria, macrophages secrete IL-12, which acts on T cells and natural killer cells (via the IL-12 receptor) to induce production of interferon-gamma. Interferon-gamma then signals through its receptor and the JAK-STAT1 pathway to activate macrophages, enhancing their capacity to kill ingested organisms and to form protective granulomas. Mutations at any point in this circuit, in the interferon-gamma receptor chains, IL-12 or its receptor, or STAT1, impair macrophage activation and granuloma formation, leaving weakly virulent mycobacteria and Salmonella able to disseminate. The narrow, well-defined nature of the defect explains the characteristic selective infection susceptibility.
additionalDifferentials: HIV/AIDS and other causes of acquired T-cell deficiency with mycobacterial disease
Severe combined immunodeficiency and combined immunodeficiencies
Disseminated tuberculosis or non-tuberculous mycobacterial infection in an immunocompetent host
additionalInvestigations: Genetic testing of the IL-12/interferon-gamma axis (IFNGR1, IFNGR2, IL12B, IL12RB1, STAT1 and related genes)
Functional assays of interferon-gamma production and receptor signalling
Flow cytometry for interferon-gamma receptor expression
Cultures and molecular identification of mycobacterial and Salmonella species
Testing for anti-interferon-gamma autoantibodies to exclude the acquired phenocopy
Imaging to define the extent of disseminated infection
redFlags: Disseminated mycobacterial or salmonella infection requiring urgent diagnosis and prolonged therapy
Disseminated BCG infection following vaccination (BCG and other live vaccines must be avoided)
Severe complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency presenting with overwhelming early infection
Recurrent or unusually severe intracellular infection prompting immunological evaluation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the molecular defect: complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency carries a poor outlook with severe, recurrent disseminated disease that responds poorly to cytokine therapy, whereas partial receptor and IL-12-axis defects often have a much better prognosis with prolonged antimycobacterial treatment and, where appropriate, adjunctive interferon-gamma.
pitfalls: Administering BCG or other live vaccines before recognising the defect, risking disseminated vaccine-strain infection
Stopping antimycobacterial therapy too early, since prolonged and sometimes lifelong treatment may be needed
Assuming a broad immunodeficiency and missing the selective nature of the defect
Overlooking the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody syndrome as a phenocopy in adults
Expecting interferon-gamma therapy to help in complete receptor deficiency
management: Treat mycobacterial and Salmonella infections with prolonged, targeted combination antimicrobial therapy, often continued long term
Give adjunctive recombinant interferon-gamma in partial receptor and IL-12-axis defects that retain interferon-gamma responsiveness
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation for complete interferon-gamma receptor deficiency, which responds poorly to cytokine therapy
Avoid live BCG and other live vaccines, and counsel on avoiding environmental mycobacterial exposure
Use long-term antimycobacterial prophylaxis to prevent recurrent disseminated infection
Provide genetic counselling and family screening for these inherited defects, distinguishing them from the acquired anti-interferon-gamma autoantibody phenocopy
Manage jointly with clinical immunology and infectious diseases, with imaging surveillance for disseminated infection
